explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Peter says, "But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed." (1 Peter 3:14) Suffering and blessing in the same sentence is a lot to chew on, but that's what the text says. And Peter wrote it to people he calls "exiles" (1 Peter 1:1).

Peter actually says the opposite. He writes, "But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed." (1 Peter 3:14) So suffering for doing right doesn't cancel the blessing. I know it sounds backwards, but that's right there in the verse.

That's it. Peter says, "But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord." (1 Peter 3:15) No building needed, no special address. This one happens right where you are, on the inside, even on a day when everything outside is rattling.

Good guess, since a temple sounds like a holy spot. But Peter says, "But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord." (1 Peter 3:15) The place he names is the heart. That means you can do it anywhere, even standing in a long line at the bank.

I see why that one tempts you, since a synagogue is a place of worship. But the verse says, "But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord." (1 Peter 3:15) Peter points to the heart, not a building. Wherever you go, your heart comes along with you.

explanations.answer: The reason for the hope in them
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Peter says to be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks "…the reason for the hope that is in you." (1 Peter 3:15) Notice it's about hope. Nobody has to win a debate, just be ready to say why they have it.

The prophets are a great subject, but that's not what Peter says here. He says to be ready to explain "…the reason for the hope that is in you." (1 Peter 3:15) So the question is about your own hope. That's a much shorter study guide than a whole history.

Whew, every law? That would take more than one afternoon, and I can't even keep up with my own oven manual. Peter says the believers should be ready to explain "…the reason for the hope that is in you." (1 Peter 3:15) The hope is the subject.

True. Peter says, "But respond with gentleness and respect…" (1 Peter 3:15) So the answer matters, and so does how it's delivered. I think a soft voice can carry a hard truth a lot farther than a loud one.

Not quite, friend. The verse says, "But respond with gentleness and respect…" (1 Peter 3:15) So Peter wants the answer given with gentleness and respect, not swung like a rolling pin. The way you say it counts too.

Yes, baker. Peter says those who slander the believers "…may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ." (1 Peter 3:16) Good behavior speaks up without raising its voice. I think that's a quiet kind of comeback.

I get the thought, since people can get steamed when they're wrong. But Peter says nothing about anger. He says they "…may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ." (1 Peter 3:16) Shame is what he names.

Louder? I think that's me on a Monday morning, not what Peter says. The verse says those who slander the believers "…may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ." (1 Peter 3:16) Good behavior is what does the work there.

Careful, friend, it's flipped around. Peter says, "For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil." (1 Peter 3:17) So suffering for doing evil is not the better one. Doing good is the side Peter wants the believers on.

Right, it's False. Peter writes, "For it is better, if it is God’s will, to suffer for doing good than for doing evil." (1 Peter 3:17) Suffering for doing good is the better of the two. Peter wants the believers to keep doing good.

That's the one. Peter says, "For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God." (1 Peter 3:18) Once. Not a repeat, not a second round. One time, and Peter says it was for the unrighteous.

I can see how a yearly thing feels familiar, like a birthday batch. But Peter says Christ "…suffered for sins once for all…" (1 Peter 3:18) Once, not on a yearly schedule. It was finished in one time.
Three is a nice number, but it's not the one here. Peter says Christ "…suffered for sins once for all…" (1 Peter 3:18) That's once. A second round isn't in the verse, and neither is a third.
True, baker. Peter says Christ suffered "…the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God." (1 Peter 3:18) That's the purpose in the text. He did it to bring the believers to God.

It's actually True. Peter says Christ suffered for sins, "…the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God." (1 Peter 3:18) Bringing the believers to God is the stated reason. That's good news worth reading twice.

I see why you'd think so, since Peter says He was put to death. But he keeps going: "He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit…" (1 Peter 3:18) So the text doesn't leave Him dead. That "but" is doing a lot of work.
Yes, False. Peter says, "He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit…" (1 Peter 3:18) He didn't stay dead. Peter says He was made alive.

Yep. Peter says God "…waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built." (1 Peter 3:20) Noah is the man God told to build the ark (Genesis 6:14). God's patience is right there in the text.

Moses is a big name, so I see the pull. He's the one who led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10). But Peter says God "…waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built." (1 Peter 3:20) Noah is the one tied to the ark here.

Elijah is a fine guess, since he was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36). But Peter says God "…waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built." (1 Peter 3:20) The ark points straight to Noah.

That's right. Peter says, "In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water." (1 Peter 3:20) Eight souls, and the water is part of how they were saved. A small number in a big story.

Fire sounds dramatic, but it's not the word. Peter says, "In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water." (1 Peter 3:20) Only eight souls, saved through water. Fire would have done a number on my bakery anyway.
Smoke is what I get when I forget the timer, so I know it well. But Peter says the eight souls "…were saved through water." (1 Peter 3:20) The word is water.
Yes, baker. Peter says, "And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also…" (1 Peter 3:21) He ties Noah's water to the believers' own day. The word he uses is baptism.

Passover, huh? I get it, that's a big one. I once tried stamping a cookie with the wrong stamper, and it came out looking like a different cookie entirely. Peter says, "And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also…" (1 Peter 3:21) Baptism is the word that fits the blank.

Sabbath! Good word, friend, but wrong cookie cutter for this blank. Peter says, "And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also…" (1 Peter 3:21) The water of Noah's day points to baptism, so that's what goes in the blank.

Close, but Peter says the opposite. He calls baptism "…not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God…" (1 Peter 3:21) So it's not about getting clean like a dish in the sink. The focus is the conscience.

Right, it's False. Peter says baptism is "…not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God…" (1 Peter 3:21) It isn't about dirt on the body. Peter points to the conscience instead.

explanations.answer: A pledge of a clear conscience toward God
explanations.explanation: You got it. Peter calls it "…the pledge of a clear conscience toward God…" (1 Peter 3:21) It's about the conscience, not about dirt. And he says it saves "…through the resurrection of Jesus Christ…"

explanations.answer: A promise to keep every law of God
explanations.explanation: I can see why that sounds serious and holy. But Peter calls baptism "…the pledge of a clear conscience toward God…" (1 Peter 3:21) He doesn't describe it as a promise to keep every law. The pledge is about a clear conscience.

explanations.answer: A record of good works before God
explanations.explanation: A record of good works sounds official, like a stack of paperwork. But Peter calls baptism "…the pledge of a clear conscience toward God…" (1 Peter 3:21) He doesn't call it a record of good works. The conscience is the focus.

That's right. Peter says Jesus "…has gone into heaven and is at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him." (1 Peter 3:22) Angels, authorities and powers are all subject to Him. That's a good place to end the passage.
Not equal, friend. Peter says Jesus is at God's right hand "…with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him." (1 Peter 3:22) Subject means they're under Him. He is over them.

I see the thought, but that isn't what this verse says. Peter says Jesus is at God's right hand "…with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him." (1 Peter 3:22) Subject to Him is the wording. Standing against Him isn't in the verse.
